ox: Incorrect. Normal sleep had the LOWEST mean reaction time (350 ms), the fastest responses.
Incorrect. The 4-hour group averaged 420 ms, which is above normal sleep but below the 2-hour group's 480 ms.
Correct. Read the table: 350, 420 and 480 ms. The largest number is 480 ms for severe sleep deprivation (2 h). Higher RT means slower, so this group was slowest.
Incorrect. The means were 420 ms and 480 ms, which are not equal; the table lists them as different values.

p: For 'which group had the highest value' questions, find the biggest number in the right column and read its row label. Reaction time is a TIME, so a bigger number means SLOWER, not better.

bp981_0.trap: Picking the middle group, or confusing a higher RT with better performance.
bp981_0.eli: Reaction time is a stopwatch: the biggest number is the slowest runner.
mem: Mean = average; SD = how spread out the individual values are.
Dose–response: more of the cause (less sleep) → more of the effect (slower RT).
bp981_0.sc: Scan the column once, circle the largest number, then read its row.
bp981_0.mn: RT = Really Tired when it's big.

ox: Incorrect. A cross-sectional survey measures sleep and scores at ONE time and only shows association; confounders (stress, illness) are not controlled.
Correct. In a randomized controlled trial, chance decides who gets each sleep condition, which balances all other factors across the groups. That is what allows a causal conclusion.
Incorrect. Case–control studies look backward and compare existing groups. They are observational and cannot show cause and effect.
Incorrect. A longitudinal cohort follows people over time but does not assign the exposure, so confounding variables remain. Following people is not the same as randomizing them.

p: Randomization is what supports causal claims. Observational designs (cross-sectional, case–control, cohort) can show association but cannot rule out confounders. The ladder of evidence for causation: randomized controlled trial > cohort > case–control > cross-sectional.

bp981_1.trap: Thinking a longitudinal cohort gives causality just because it follows participants over time.
bp981_1.eli: Flipping a coin to decide who gets less sleep makes the groups alike in every other way, so any difference in the result must come from the sleep.
mem: RCT = random assignment = best for CAUSE and effect.
Confounder: a third variable that explains the link.
bp981_1.sc: See the word 'randomly assigned' and think causal.

ox: Correct. Top-down processing uses context, memory, and expectation to interpret input. The sentence helps you read the misspelled word.
Wrong. Bottom-up starts with raw features such as lines and edges and builds up. Trap: the misspelling alone would make bottom-up reading hard.
Wrong. Parallel processing means handling many features at the same time. It does not describe using context. Trap: confusing a mechanism with a direction.
Wrong. Feature detection is the bottom-up step of picking out lines and edges. Trap: mixing this with expectation-driven reading.

p: Bottom-up processing starts with the raw sensory data and builds toward a perception. Top-down processing starts with knowledge and expectations that shape how data are read.
When context helps you read a misspelled word, your brain is filling in the answer from what it already knows. That is top-down.

q93.eli: Guessing a word in a story from the sentence around it, rather than sounding out every letter.
mem: Parallel processing = many features at once
q93.trap: If context or experience guides perception, choose top-down.
q93.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The law of proximity says items that are close together are seen as a group.
Wrong. Similarity groups items that look alike, such as same color or shape. Here the cue is closeness. Trap: mixing up the two grouping cues.
Wrong. Closure fills in gaps so you see a complete shape. Trap: the 'gaps' idea can sound like distance.
Wrong. Continuity prefers smooth, continuous lines or paths. Trap: dots in a row can suggest a line, but here grouping is by closeness.

p: Gestalt psychology says the brain organizes parts into whole patterns. Several rules explain how we group things.
Proximity groups near items. Similarity groups alike items. Closure fills gaps. Continuity follows smooth lines.

q94.eli: Kids standing close together at recess look like one team, even if they wear different shirts.
q94.trap: Find the cue in the stem. 'Close together' always means proximity.
q94.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Even though you were not attending to that conversation, your brain still processed it enough to catch your name. This is the cocktail party effect and shows unattended input gets some processing.
Wrong. You were not following that conversation, so this is not divided attention. Trap: being able to hear something does not mean you were attending to it.
Wrong. Inattentional blindness is failing to notice something visible because attention is elsewhere. Here you did notice. Trap: confusing failure to notice with noticing.
Wrong. Change blindness is missing a change in a scene. Nothing changed here. Trap: confusing attention-related terms.

concept.t: Selective attention and the cocktail party effect
p: Selective attention means focusing on one input and filtering out others. The cocktail party effect is hearing your own name or something important in a conversation you were ignoring.
This suggests unattended input is not fully blocked. It is partly analyzed for meaning, which fits attenuation models of attention.

q95.eli: Chatting with a friend in a crowd, then turning your head when someone across the room says your name.
mem: Cocktail party effect = hearing your name in an ignored conversation
Inattentional blindness = missing visible things when attention is elsewhere
q95.trap: Do not confuse noticing an ignored stimulus with the failures of attention such as inattentional or change blindness.
q95.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. REM sleep has vivid dreams, muscle atonia (temporary loss of muscle tone), and fast, wake-like EEG waves. It is also called paradoxical sleep.
Wrong. NREM stage 3 is slow-wave sleep with delta waves, the deepest NREM stage. Trap: deep sleep is not dreaming sleep.
Wrong. Stage 1 is light sleep with theta waves, as you drift off. Trap: the EEG slows here, not wake-like.
Wrong. Stage 2 has sleep spindles and K-complexes. Trap: it is the longest stage, but not the dreaming one.

p: Sleep alternates between NREM stages 1 to 3 and REM. EEG is a recording of brain waves.
REM is the stage when most vivid dreaming occurs. Muscles are paralyzed so you do not act out dreams, and the brain waves look like those of wakefulness.

q96.eli: In REM the brain is busy like it is awake, but the body is switched off, like a movie playing on a remote-controlled TV.
mem: REM: dreams, atonia, wake-like beta/low-voltage EEG
Stage 1: theta; Stage 2: spindles and K-complexes
q96.mn: REM = Rapid Eye Movement. Also remember 'paradoxical sleep': the brain looks awake, but the body is paralyzed.
q96.trap: Wake-like EEG plus paralysis points to REM, not any NREM stage.
q96.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology and neuroscience texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The NEW phone number (learned later) blocks recall of the OLD one. New learning reaching backward to disrupt old memory is retroactive interference.
Proactive interference is the reverse: an OLD memory blocks learning or recall of NEW information. Here the new number is blocking the old one, so direction is the trap.
Decay says memories fade just from time and disuse. The question gives a specific cause (learning a new number), which points to interference, not simple fading.
Source amnesia means remembering a fact but forgetting where you learned it. You are failing to recall the old number itself, not its source.

p: Interference means one memory gets in the way of another. Retroactive interference: new information disrupts old information. Proactive interference: old information disrupts new information.
Retro means backward, pro means forward. Ask: which memory is being blocked? If the old one is blocked, it is retroactive.

q97.eli: It is like writing a new phone number over an old one on the same sticky note. The new writing makes the old writing hard to read.
mem: Decay = fading from time alone; source amnesia = forgetting where you learned it
q97.mn: Retro = Reaches back to erase old; Pro = Pushes forward to block new.
q97.trap: Mixing up the direction of interference. Find which memory is hard to recall: old blocked means retroactive.
q97.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Conservation (amount stays the same when shape changes) develops in the concrete operational stage, about ages 7 to 11. The child reasons logically about real, concrete objects.
Preoperational children (about 2 to 7) are fooled by appearance. They say the taller glass has more water. Failing conservation is the hallmark of this stage.
Sensorimotor (birth to about 2) is about learning through senses and movement, and object permanence. Conservation tasks are far beyond this stage.
Formal operational (about 12 and up) is abstract and hypothetical reasoning. Conservation is already mastered earlier, so it does not define this stage.

p: Piaget described four stages of thinking: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational. Conservation means knowing that quantity stays the same even if the shape or look changes.
A child who passes the water-glass test is using logic about real objects. That is concrete operational thinking.

q98.eli: A younger kid thinks a squished ball of clay is 'less' than a round one. An older kid knows it is the same clay, just a new shape.
mem: Concrete operational 7-11: conservation, logic about real things
Formal operational 12+: abstract and hypothetical thinking
q98.mn: Piaget stages: Sensorimotor, Preoperational, Concrete operational, Formal operational. Remember 'Some People Can Fly' (S, P, C, F).
q98.trap: Choosing preoperational because the task involves a child. Passing conservation means the child is already past preoperational.
q98.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Recalling the first items (primacy effect, moved into long-term memory by rehearsal) and the last items (recency effect, still in short-term memory) together is the serial position effect.
The spacing effect means studying spread over time beats cramming. It is about study schedules, not which list positions are remembered.
Chunking groups items into larger units (like splitting a phone number) to increase capacity. It does not explain better recall of the ends of a list.
Priming is when earlier exposure to a stimulus unconsciously changes a later response. It does not describe position in a list.

p: When you learn a list, you remember the beginning and the end best, and the middle worst. Memory for the beginning is the primacy effect. Memory for the end is the recency effect.
Early items get more rehearsal and reach long-term memory. Last items are still fresh in short-term memory.

q99.eli: When you hear a long list of chores, you remember the first one and the last one, but the ones in the middle blur together.
mem: Primacy = long-term memory; recency = short-term memory
q99.trap: Picking the spacing effect because it also sounds like a memory-timing idea. Spacing is about study sessions, not list position.
q99.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.
